maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to take advantage of the study of the estimates of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to call the attention of the minister to a matter which concerns Indian affairs in particular.
At the outset of his remarks this morning, the minister told us that the government entrusted him with the responsibility of Indian affairs about a year ago. In view of the changes being effected by that department in the area that I represent and where I live, I feel that the minister should also answer to the house for the activities of his departmental officials.
The minister advised me recently in writing of the official decision to transfer the Indian affairs office from Amos to Val d'Or. I had been aware for several weeks that the department of Indian affairs wanted this transfer and I was also aware, having been involved personally, that steps were taken on both sides. I was involved in the steps taken by the authorities and by the public bodies of Amos to keep this office in Amos where it has been for more than 25 years. I wondered why this transfer was being made from one city to another in this northwestern region. After analysing all reasons that were given to me and to the representative of the town of Amos, I concluded that it was more a question of accommodating the civil servants than giving the Indians the service the department is required to give them.
On February 8, I received from the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Laing) a letter giving the reasons supplied by his officials to ask for such transfer. Here is what he said, and I quote:
It has been suggested that the main office of a new division which will serve the whole northwestern part of the province, be set up at Val d'Or.
Supply-Indian Affairs
I would like to know who made that suggestion. The minister does not say who did in his letter; he merely says, "It has been suggested". I would therefore like to know who made the suggestion, whether it was the Indians themselves, the leaders of the Indian bands in the area or officials who, for some reason I do not know exactly, prefer living in one city rather than in the other.
The minister also pointed out to me that, according to his officials' reports, and I quote:
Val d'Or has an airport which gives regular service towards Poste-de-la-Baleine and other points, and I understand that that was one of the factors which the branch officials took into consideration.
On January 24, 1967, the clerk of the town of Amos, on behalf of the municipal corporation of Amos, sent a letter to the assistant deputy minister of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in which he said in part:
The town of Amos has now almost completed the municipal airport started a few years ago and air traffic could begin as early as next summer-
Meaning this summer.
-since the landing-ground itself is more than sufficient.
Mr. Chairman, as far as the airport is concerned, I think the problem can be solved shortly and I know that representations are being made by the authorities of the town of Amos with the Department of Transport for the completion of that airport.
So, I continue reading the reasons given by the minister in his letter of February 8:
Moreover, Val d'Or is more central since it is linked by road with Maniwaki and Notre-Dame-du-Nord.
With Maniwaki, right, but it is not quite the same thing as far as Notre-Dame-du-Nord is concerned because to get there

if my information is correct; I live in the area-one must pass by Rouyn, and from Rouyn, the distance to Amos or Val d'Or is about the same. Therefore, only the Maniwaki area would have the distance advantage. On the other hand, the Matagami and La Sarre areas and others to the north would be at a disadvantage, because their residents would have to travel farther to go to the Val d'Or office, whenever the need arises. The letter goes on to say:
The need to expand the office so that it may serve as a regional office is not, it seems, an important aspect of the question, for this need could be met in both places.

June 9, 1S67
Supply-Indian Affairs
That is true, tor a letter was sent to an official of the department living in Rouyn to tell him that there were unoccupied buildings in the town of Amos which were large enough to house these offices, and that if these buildings did not meet the needs of the department, a number of Amos businessmen would undertake to build others within a short time.
I continue to quote the minister's letter:
However, I am told that it could more easily be done in Val d'Or.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Therefore, do not think it is easier to put up public buildings in Val d'Or than in Amos. Sometimes, it is building contractors from Amos who erect buildings in Val d'Or.
I continue:
As far as living accommodation for the staff is concerned, Val d'Or, being a larger town, has more facilities; that is one thing which should be taken into consideration, because staff recruitment can be hindered at times because of a lack of accommodation for rent at reasonable prices.
Here is what the tour clerk of Amos wrote to the deputy minister on January 24:
The matter has been referred to the municipal authorities which intend to facilitate access to appropriate housing to employees of your department; at any rate, several large projects are anticipated for the spring. The town of Amos is developing rapidly and will certainly be able to provide accommodation immediately, and even better this summer, for all additional employees your department may need in Amos.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I think that meets the requirements of the Indian affairs branch as far as offices and housing for the staff in that city are concerned.
In his letter to me, the minister said:
The proposed district will include Indian people of different languages and religious faiths. To meet their needs and to provide them with our services in the most acceptable manner, it can be expected that some members of the staff of the proposed district office will also be of different origins and request, for themselves and their families, schools and churches which exist in Val d'Or but not in Amos.
Mr. Chairman, there again, I feel that as far as education and religious services are concerned, the city of Amos can meet the needs of any nationality just as well as any other city in northwestern Quebec. As a matter of fact, in his letter of January 24 which I quoted earlier, the Amos city clerk mentioned this with regard to schools:
The city has several primary and secondary schools and is also the headquarters of the Harri-cana regional school board which controls the whole secondary educational system in the area. Amos

also has an Institute of Higher Studies, soon to be certified by the provincial government, which prepares students to enter university.
The Indian population of Amos is already integrated in the city of Amos and its religious and cultural institutions, and every day, young Indians can be seen fraternizing with the white population of the city. We submit that the educational experiment of the Indian affairs branch in Amos has been very successful and that the prevailing educational climate in Amos is unique in northwestern Quebec.
Eventually, the city of Amos will be in a position to accommodate all the Indian students from the north of the province and provide English classes for them, since several requests have already been made by English-speaking families who wish to settle in Amos and are only waiting for the establishment of English schools to do so.
Mr. Chairman, now that could meet the requirements mentioned by the department officials to justify transferring the office?
In the light of the reasons given by those officials and the services which are planned at Amos, as well as at Val d'Or and everywhere else, I have come to the conclusion that it is not so much that the Indians want to settle in Amos but rather that civil servants want to ensure their own well-being instead of wanting to serve the Indians who come under the jurisdiction of the department.
Last summer I accompanied the committee on northern affairs and national resources on a tour of northern Canada, the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, and I found that in those places too there are civil servants who do not seem to understand why they are there.
Of all places we visited, I noticed that the community where this situation was most obvious was the town of Fort Smith where, it seemed to me, nobody cared about Indians or Indian affairs.
I also noticed that civil servants, in that town especially, were mainly concerned with their own welfare. They are helping Indians to ensure their comfort, but as far as their education or their care is concerned, they almost completely forget about them, to the extent that when we held meetings at Fort Smith, all the Indians and Eskimos who must live in that area, I imagine, were absent, except a half-breed I think.
All that to say, Mr. Chairman, that reforms would probably be needed within the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to ensure proper administration of Indian affairs.
Those are, Mr. Chairman, the comments I wanted to address to the minister this afternoon. I would also ask him once again who requested that transfer of office from Amos to
June 9, 1967

Val d'Or. Could he tell us, at the same time, whether the Indians, individually or through their chiefs, have asked for that transfer or whether they have been consulted? In the latter case, how was it done and what was their reply? It would be interesting to know the answers to those questions.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
I should like to begin my remarks, Mr. Chairman, by thanking the minister for his statement at the commencement of this discussion. He touched on three major areas of his department, national parks, Indian affairs and northern administration. In the few minutes allotted to him, as he stated, he was unable to deal with these subjects in the depth he would have liked. In my view the remarks he made regarding resource development in the Northwest Territories were amongst the most significant.
However, for the moment I should like to talk about Indian affairs. Earlier this week I had the opportunity of visiting the Canadian Indian pavilion at Expo '67. This pavilion, which was sponsored by the minister's department, was designed and developed by the Indian people themselves. I believe every Canadian who visits Expo should take the hour necessary to visit it. It tells completely the story of the Indian people and their association with the white man from the time the white man first came to this continent. The department provided the funds for the construction of the pavilion but told the Indian people, this is your pavilion and you tell us what you think it should be like.
I believe the most significant thing about the pavilion is the story it tells and the indication of a change in attitude toward the administration of Indian affairs because the government said, "We want you to do it." The story told is not necessarily a happy one. When you walk into the building you feel the bewilderment that the Indian people must have felt when they first encountered the white man on this continent. Then there is an indication of some semblance of hope that they could live with the white man. As the white man expanded westward there was a feeilng of despair and frustration, and finally hate. We see the effect of the white man's institutions on the Indian people and their culture.
However, as you walk out you see the story of what is happening in terms of Indian education today. As you leave you feel that the Indian people believe this may be a time of change and the white man and his red-skin
Supply-Indian Affairs brother may be able to live together on this continent. I was rather impressed upon reading some of the inscriptions on the walls of the building. In the early days the Indian people said:
We paid honour to the spirits in all living things by wasting nothing.
This is so symbolic of the culture of the Indian people. On the other hand, there were some words that were rather harsh and bitter, not the least of which were these:
Well into the twentieth century the welfare of the Indian was regarded as proper work for retired soldiers, many of whom were kindly and well intentioned but treated their charges like amiable,' backward children.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
I hope that this pavilion and the story it tells are an indication of a change of attitude, a change in approach on the part of individuals generally with respect to their relationship toward the Indian people. In this respect I should like to draw the attention of the committee for a moment treaties Nos. 8 and II which affect the Indians of the Northwest Territories, northern British Columbia, northern Alberta and northern Saskatchewan. These treaties were signed in the 1920's. Certain agreements were made between the Indian people and the Queen, including the disposition of certain lands to the Indian people. To this day these treaties have never been fulfilled in that the Indian people, who incidentally do not want to live on reserves in these areas, have never received compensation in lieu of the lands they were to receive.
At Inuvik last week I spoke with Mr. James Koe, a member of the Indian advisory committee, about treaties 8 and 11. Mr. Koe expressed to me a feeling of incredible confusion, distrust and lack of understanding regarding the position of the Indians with respect to these treaties. The treaties themselves were obviously written in a hurry by meandering bands of well intentioned civil servants who were sent to negotiate some form of arrangement with the Indian people.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: What year were the treaties signed?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
The treaties were signed in 1921. An example of the kind of confusion is that one of the terms in treaty 11 is the provision of $3 worth of shells, nets and other paraphernalia needed for the Indian way of life. In 1921 this amount may have been significant. Today the Indian people are still receiving $3 worth but instead of five or six

June 9, 1967
Supply-Indian Affairs boxes of shells and one or two fish nets they receive perhaps one box of shells and one fish net for every second family. I am hopeful that the department and the minister will resolve to treat the problems facing our northern Indian people as urgent and will discuss with them the provisions contained in treaties 8 and 11, which to date has not been done.
When I had the opportunity of saying a few words in the debate on the speech from the throne I touched on a subject which I believe is of great importance in the development of the country to the north. I refer to the provision of basic services to the communities there. I spoke at great length about the extension of adequate water and sewer services to the community of Inuvik. I must congratulate the minister and his department in that within three or four days of my speech they were able to announce the start of an experimental system at Inuvik. I know this was not necessarily as a result of the few remarks I made because I understand that action was under way prior to the debate in the house. However, I think this is an important matter which must be faced by the government of Canada together with the governments in the territories, both territorial and municipal.
In the process of transferring responsibility from the federal government to the territorial government I would like to see arrangements made whereby the senior government would take upon itself responsibility for initiating and establishing an adequate water supply, sewage disposal, electricity and basic housing in all northern communities. This is an opportunity for the federal government to show the seriousness with which it intends to develop and is developing the north. It seems to me that this would be a logical, reasonable and practical step.
In the process of opening up northern Canada communications and transportation are two of the obvious factors of great importance. The minister made reference this morning to the fact that within the last several weeks two air lines commenced operating jet equipment to the Arctic coast. This is true and it is a good thing. It is an example of the initiative that can be taken in the north by the private operator or entrepreneur.
However, Mr. Chairman, one of the difficulties with which we are faced is the development of adequate facilities. In many parts of northern Canada and the northern part of many provinces there are periods of the year when communities are completely cut off

from the outside. These periods vary from three to six to nine weeks, at break up and again at freeze-up. Apart from the obvious dangers that could arise as a result of epidemics, the over-all growth and development of these areas is greatly affected.
Yesterday I received a telephone call from a community in Keewatin called Eskimo Point. The object of the call was to see whether somehow or other the backlog of mail which apparently exists in Churchill could be moved out very quickly as the break-up was expected in two or three days. Fortunately the post office was one step ahead of us and there was no need to follow up this matter. But the point is that sometimes those in the south forget that a community of 200, 300 or 400 people can be completely cut off from the outside for a period of time.
The point I am trying to make is that there is urgent need for the development of adequate air strips in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory, as well as in other areas of Canada which at times are isolated and cut off from the rest of the country. I know the minister has proposed an air strip program which would bring year round transportation facilities to every community for which he is responsible. I know that this program has had some rough sledding at the hands of members of the Treasury Board. However, I should like to add my words of support in the strongest way for this program, with the hope that the minister will be able to convince his cabinet colleagues that the only way we will develop this great northern country of our is to provide adequate transportation and communication services to meet the growing needs.
Within the past several months it was announced that Yellowknife had been selected as the capital of the Northwest Territories. It was also announced that the commissioner of the Northwest Territories would move to the capital of Yellowknife. We are all anxiously looking forward to seeing the legislation brought before the house to bring about the development of responsible government in the Northwest Territories.
A few days ago I said I hoped that the legislation would be in line with the views of the people who live in these territories so that it will be passed readily by the house. There will be a certain amount of discussion of what the government is proposing and I suggest to the minister that there are three areas which he might want to consider before such legislation is brought before the house.
June 9, 1967

[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
The first matter is the relationship between the commissioner of the Northwest Territories and the minister. If I might explain under the present legislation the commissioner is responsible to the minister and at the same time he is the head of a partly elected and partly appointed council. As such he is in the rather awkward position of having to keep the minister happy and having to keep the elected representatives happy. He serves two masters, which is awkward. I have no patent solution to the problem and I do not intend to bring one forward today, but I ask the minister to keep in mind what I have said when bringing down his proposals.
The second matter that the minister ought to consider is the amount of indemnity that is to be paid to members of the territorial council. Approximately one year ago we enacted legislation which raised the salaries of the elected members of the council from $2,000 to $5,000 a year. We also agreed to pay $3,500 a year to the appointed members. At that time it was said that these changes were housekeeping amendments. If we expect the elected representatives to bear responsibility in the territorial government I do not think it should be up to this house to set their salaries. We should not say what the elected representatives are to be paid. I sincerely and firmly believe that if the members of the council decide to raise their own salaries beyond what is reasonable they will receive their answer from the electorate. The next time round they may be looking for a new job.
The third point that I hope the minister will take into account when he brings in this legislation has to do with the appointed members of the council. I know there are compelling arguments for having appointed members for the time being on the Northwest Territories council to represent the views of all Canadians, because the federal government itself has a great interest in the north. But what the government seeks to achieve can be achieved as effectively, or possibly more so, by establishing a series of advisory groups or committees which would report to the commissioner with respect to those areas on which the appointed members now report. I suggest that the minister consider my proposals so that when the legislation is brought forward all aspects of it can be examined in a non-partisan manner. This would be in the best interests of the two territories in the northern part of Canada.
Supply-Indian Affairs
I was interested in the reactions of many hon. members who have already spoken on parks. They said nothing new, having repeated their ideas on many occasions and in various committee meetings. The one area I wish to bring to the minister's attention is the Wood Buffalo national park. We have heard the minister acknowledge that if, somehow or other, the federal government and the province of Alberta could get together arrangements might be worked out whereby certain areas of the park would be transferred to the province and be administered by it. These areas include the so-called gypsum deposit which along the Peace river and the timber stands in the same area. The northeastern corner of Alberta, as a result of the tar sands development, has become a centre of new economic activity and resource development. When these arrangements I have spoken of are worked out between the federal and provincial governments I expect that the economic activity will extend virtually to the border of the Northwest Territories.
My point is that there has been much talking about this subject. I do not know at what level that talking has taken place but the newspapers have had much to say about the matter. I do know that it is important to resolve the discussions between the two levels of government as quickly as possible. There seems to be a tendency for each of the governments concerned to say: "Well, if you will come to us with a proposal we will be prepared to listen to you without making any commitment." I am not skilled in the arts of diplomacy and negotiation but I am sure that somehow or other arrangements could be worked out to bring about an agreement to transfer part of Wood Buffalo national park to the Alberta government.
In this our centennial year all Canadians should take great pride in what is happening in the Northwest Territories and in the Yukon Territory. I listened this morning to the remarks of the former minister of this department and to his biased platitudes about what he and his government had done when they were in office. We acknowledge that there was an impetus to do what they did. We also acknowledge that the roads program, for example, in the north was an extension of plans which were already on the drawing board. We are aware that in the years 1962 and 1963, when an austerity program was implemented, that the unfortunate area to be hit first and hardest was northern Canada. Millions of dollars for the construction of roads and schools

June 9. 1987
Supply-Indian Affairs disappeared from the estimates. Only in the last two or three years have programs to achieve what should have been achieved come back on the rails. These programs have been added to the new programs.
Be that as it may, I am hopeful that we have started on a course which will develop the great natural resources of the north. We hope that any such program will involve the people of the north in the development of their natural resources. Mr. Chairman, the greatest asset that we have in northern Canada is our people.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as a member of the committee on northern affairs and national resources in the last session of parliament I feel compelled to offer a few remarks at this time. Having been a member of the expedition composed of committee members, the deputy minister and officials of the northern affairs department which toured the Northwest Territories and the Yukon from July 28 to August 8 last, I believe that as a result of this tour we now take more interest in these territories, their peoples and in their administration than we did previously. We feel closer to these people.
I had never been in the Arctic before. I marvelled at the magnitude of that land, its emptiness, the bleak loneliness of the north. I also learned to appreciate the unique beauty of the hardy life which, none the less, does flourish there. In a 15-minute walk across the tundra just outside the village of Frobisher Bay I picked ten different kinds of beautiful wild flowers unknown to the rest of Canada. I also noted during that walk that the white man is defiling the north. We left our bus along the road to take pictures of a beautiful bed of wild flowers outside the village of Frobisher Bay and we found proof that the white man is littering the north as he is littering the south. I had to pick up a couple of empty beer bottles from that flower bed before I could take a picture of those beautiful Arctic wild flowers.
I maintain that we as Canadians must govern ourselves in the north in such a way as to avoid what has happened in other parts of Canada or we shall find the north polluted and defiled, something which should never be allowed to happen. I mention this in passing, and I know the minister agrees with me in this regard.
I congratulate the minister on having arranged this "first ever" trip. It was the first time a committee of the House of Commons

had visited the vast far north. I thank the deputy minister, Mr. Gordon, the northern administrator, Mr. Henderson, and the other officials who accompanied us for the vast amount of information they were able to impart to the members of our committee. I also thank all my travelling companions for a very pleasant journey in such distinguished and agreeable company. I also wish to thank formally the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Fort William, who gave us such good leadership during our journey.
The next expedition to be made north of the 60th parallel, which is the southern boundary of these territories, should consist of the Prime Minister and all his cabinet colleagues. They would then waken up and become cognizant of the shortcomings of the present government with respect to the needs of these territories and their peoples. If they were to take such a trip their attention would be diverted from subjects on which they have been wasting time for the past three years, namely, flags, national anthems, political inquiries, coats of arms, bilingualism and other matters which divide Canada and distract public attention from the shortcomings and blunders of the present administration in other and more important fields of their grave responsibility, including the Arctic.
As a member of the committee I appreciated the meetings we held every evening in each northern centre we visited. I will outline some of the needs expressed, some of the progress made and some of the comments, both favourable and unfavourable, advanced by the Eskimos and the Indians. At Frobisher Bay we met with the Eskimos in Apex Hill hall which is in the Eskimo village of Apex Hill just outside the town of Frobisher Bay. Hon. members will be proud to learn that this hall was built by the Imperial Order of the Daughters of the Empire. It filled my breast with pride to read the sign outside the hall linking this illustrious order with the needs of the north. I thought of the tremendous influence for good which the Daughters of the Empire and all other patriotic Canadian ladies' organizations have exercised in the building of Canada.
One of the things which concerned the community council was the need for more adult education for Eskimos. Members of the committee will recall that the council protested the building of a government liquor store at Frobisher Bay. Most council members said it would have been better to build a radio station at Resolute Bay. They told the committee that a good radio station covering the
June 9, 1967

eastern Arctic would help serve as a classroom for the educational program they wanted. A good 10,000 watt transmitter would pay off in this regard. The government could see to it that receivers were issued to all residents and knowledge would be imparted by radio courses to these potentially adept and receptive people the year round, especially during the long months of the Arctic night. Members of the community council pointed out that though southern Canada now has colour television 40 per cent of Canada and the 30,000 people of the Northwest Territories do not even enjoy satisfactory radio transmission.
Medical services at Frobisher were said to be good, and I compliment the minister and his department on this. But the remainder of the eastern Arctic depends on the ship C. D. Howe which once a year brings medical attention to outports near Arctic waterways. The C. D. Howe costs $15,000 a day to operate and we were told that last year it was stuck in the ice for about 15 days during which time, of course, people were getting no benefit from its services.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: When I have finished.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: What about the nursing stations?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Most of the council agreed that it might be better to have a flying doctor service, especially on Baffin island.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: They have one.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
I hope they have one by now. They did not have one at the time I mentioned. I am only reporting some of the shortcomings of this government, some of the conditions about which these people were rightly complaining. A flying doctor service costs less than a marine service and would be more efficient.
* (4:00 p.m.)
In order to establish tourism in the eastern Arctic it would be necessary to have concerted community development and a very careful policy. I do know there are many United States citizens who would like to tour the Arctic, especially the eastern Arctic. I believe there is a potential, especially in the Baffin island area, which in time could be cultivated.
I was informed that the Eskimo natives are crying for more work to do in their homes
Supply-Indian Affairs and in their fur garment and sealskin industry. I was advised that vast amounts of money are being wasted in the north in relation to welfare payments. Apparently many of the native recipients just sit around drawing relief. Their dumps get bigger and bigger, and so do the welfare payments. One Eskimo member of the council, when speaking to us at Frobisher Bay last July, said "Do not give us something we do not know what to do with; give us something that we know or can learn about, and how to use". That is pretty plain English. As someone said, it is not necessary to be among these people very long before they are able to impart to you knowledge which applies to them and about which one could not know from any other source.
When one learns to know the way the Eskimos think it is possible to appreciate what they mean. There also seemed to be an inference that the Eskimos, compared to their affluent white fellow citizens, are many levels lower in the community. One Eskimo woman stood up and spoke to the meeting. These people are very eloquent. They have an inborn innate quality which enables them to express themselves very articulately. This woman voiced the opinion that there was too much difference between the white people and the Eskimos. She said that the white people are served their fuel oil while the Eskimo people must go where the oil is kept and carry it home in a pail.
I also learned there is a big difference between the pay and the living conditions of personnel of the Department of Transport and personnel of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in the Northwest Territories. For example, personnel of the Department of Transport fare 25 per cent better than their counterparts in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in this regard. I was told that over the past three years personnel in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development have actually suffered a cut in wages because of the rapidly rising cost of living which we have been talking about here for the past year, and in respect of which the government has done nothing.
I have said that we must bring to the Eskimo people more needed medical services. On October 18 I pointed out to the house that there is a lack of medical services at Pond Inlet, a village of 250 people, and at Clyde River, an Eskimo village of 240 people on the northeast coast of Baffin island. These medical services are needed at those points immediately. Surely by now this problem has

June 9, 1967
Supply-Indian Affairs been taken care of by the minister and his officials.
The council at Frobisher Bay was critical of the government housekeeping. It was said that the administration allows the dumping of sewage at high water near the Apex Hill housing settlement. This must be corrected and stopped. A councillor, named Tick-abick-and the hon. member for the Northwest Territories probably will remember him, because I believe he is an acquaintance- protested the fact that white people have freezers and the Eskimos are not allowed to have them. He said they might not be required in winter, but that they are required in summer because this is the time when more animals are available and can be frozen for food to be used later.
Another councillor, named Uladjuk, deplored the fact that the council has no power and should be able to do more than just sit around and talk. I am sure that all of the members of this house agree with Uladjuk. The Eskimos at Cambridge Bay require more financing for their local co-operative. An Eskimo woman who was in the audience at the Cambridge Bay meeting said that times are changing very fast as Eskimo ways change to the white man's ways. This woman too was very eloquent which, as I said before, is something common to the Eskimo race. She said she is encouraging her children to stay in school in order to learn more of the modern ways of the great outside world.
At Cambridge Bay the medical services are good. There are five nurses in the field, three doctors, and one hospital with 26 beds serving 3,000 people on the island. I should like to remind hon. members that this island, Victoria island, is a territory larger than Newfoundland.
So much for some of the needs of the Eskimos. As I told the house on October 18, the public health nurse who looks after the Dog Rib Indian tribe at Fort MacPherson needs a means to transport her patients from the outlying points to the nursing station and often to the landing stage of the Peel river. Many hon. members who have visited this area can vouch for this need. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni was with me at the time I was discussing this small but very important need at that village. I would hope that by this time the administration and the minister have arranged for the provision of a car at Fort MacPherson on the Peel river.
When speaking of the Indians, Mr. Chairman, I remember when I was a child hearing

one of the first Indian songs I ever heard. It is known as the Indian Lament. Many members probably remember it. I should like to quote the first verse of this song, because it is so true in relation to the subject we are discussing this afternoon:
An old Indian sat in his birch bark canoe And sailed o'er the waters so deep and so blue And he sang of the time when the lands were their own
Before the pale faced men among them were known.
This lament went on through many verses to commemorate the tragedy of their race.
The story of the North American Indian is one of the greatest tragedies in modern history. We found this to be the case when we visited certain sections of the north which were populated by Indians. Their plight is regrettable. The Indians at Churchill are in a very poor state. When we visited their village, their low standard of living, which is largely self inflicted, was evident. We went up a road flanked on either side by what once were neat and comfortably built government houses. These houses were recently built. They did not appear to be much over five years old. I did not see one house in which the windows were intact. This village was a real slum. It is a disgrace, not necessarily to the natives, but to us, to the people of Canada and to those of us who sit in this chamber and endeavour to administrate, e (4:10 p.m.)
The chief of that tribe just outside the town of Churchill apologized because of the broken windows in his house. He said that he did not break them but that they were broken by the younger generation who, since the tribe left the bush five years ago, had no respect whatever for tribal authority. I can see a parallel in this in relation to younger generations in other parts of Canada. These Indian young people will no longer respect civil or tribal authority. Let me commend the government for correcting this situation by moving this village to a point four miles outside the town near the Eskimo village, but I hope this is not just an act of sweeping the dust under the rug. Perhaps this will improve the lot of this Chippewan tribe of Indians outside of Churchill.
The Prime Minister has said that the Company of Young Canadians would be employed in social and citizenship work among the Indians of Canada during this our centennial year. It is my understanding that this group now consists of 112 young Canadians,
June 9, 1967

66 of whom are volunteers and 46 administrators. It seems to me that in this case there are more chiefs than Indians. Surely this situation does not augur well for the future of this Company of Young Canadians. Apparently there is a shortage in recruitment for this company of 2,400. The Prime Minister suggested that the group should comprise 2,500. It has been forecast that this company will spend $2,445,000 in carrying out its activities this year. On the basis of the number now in this company this figure works out to about $38,000 per volunteer, and 12 cents per citizen in Canada including those unfortunate Chippewan Indians who are supposed to be helped. Apparently this group of young Canadians, for which we all hold great hopes, has had little success. I do not blame the minister for this situation, but I do draw it to the attention of the Prime Minister and the cabinet.
The chief of this tribe of Chippewans has said that their greatest problem results from Indians drinking alcoholic beverages in the town of Churchill. Apparently they go into the town, partake of these beverages and then return home and destroy property. Let me ask the eternal question: Why do we aid and abet this terrible curse on these people? These were once proud Indians who have now lost all their inbred initiative as a result of the white man providing them with alcohol. We have been told that when the Indians could not buy alcohol from the white man they made their own. This problem must be solved if these once proud people are to survive, but apparently this government is doing nothing to find a solution.
At this point I should like to emphasize the need to continue the roads to resources program initiated by the former Conservative government under the sound leadership of Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker. This program has paid off and the Pine Point railway development is living proof of that fact. I marvel at the work being done in that area and the wealth being wrested from the north and transported by that railway to markets in the south. I know that this is our most famous road to resources. Last year 185 men produced $55 million in new wealth from this northern area. I do not know what the figures are for the current year, but it is likely proportionately greater. This wealth has come from the movement of concentrates and other materials from that area to all parts of the continent.
Supply-Indian Affairs
Having regard to this railway let me remind the Minister of Transport that I noted a number of unprotected level crossings on this line, some of which were in the town of Hay River. There is quite a bit of automobile traffic in that area and these people are entitled to safety signals at these railway crossings, just as we in the southern part of the country are entitled to them. Last spring I warned the government about the folly of building new railway lines with unprotected crossings, and my remarks in this regard can be found at pages 4270 and 4271 of Hansard for that session. One might find some excuse for the lack of safety signals at level crossings on well-established lines which were built before the advent of automobile transportation, but there is no excuse for unprotected level crossings on newly constructed railway lines. On those lines every crossing should be protected. These protections should be as basic to the construction of railway lines as ties, rails and rolling stock.
In closing, let me express the hope that this government will awaken to the needs of the north and the value to Canada that this vast area could become. Let all Canadians recognize this fact and devote themselves to the development of this last and largest geographical and physical frontier of this country. We cannot all live in a narrow strip within sight of the great lakes or the 49th parallel. Let us bury the things that divide us along this narrow strip I have mentioned, and walk a little further northward in the unity that we owe this great land. We must do so if we are to develop it fully for posterity.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I too would like to make a few remarks on the estimates of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Laing).
As the member for the largest riding in Canada, that of my hon. colleague and friend from the Northwest Territories (Mr. Orange) excepted, of course, I must say that there are several problems in my riding concerning not only the Indians but the Eskimos as well; some also stem from the tremendous size of northern Canada and the Quebec part of it in particular.
Mr. Chairman, my riding covers 375,000 square miles and has a population of 128,000. Needless to say, problems often arise which are very complex. I have already mentioned this area a few times in the house and I insist on mentioning it again.

June 9, 1967
Supply-Indian Affairs
The northern part of my constituency is inhabited by most of the Indian and Eskimo population of the Quebec far north. Nevertheless, Mr. Chairman, I should like to mention here what has been done for certain Indian reservations, because extensive work has been undertaken recently and I would like at this stage the thank and congratulate the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development for his great understanding of these problems, and his staff for their initiative, particularly for the program which I would call the five-year home building plan launched two years ago in the renewal of certain Indian reservations of Canada.
I must also mention that my constituency includes eight official Indian reservations partly composed of the Montagnais tribe, the Naskopis and the Eskimos. These reservations are situated at Les Escoumins, Bersimis, Sept-Iles, Maliotenam, Schefferville, Mingan, Pointe-Parent, and La Romaine.
In the Bersimis reservation, several houses and schools have already been built and other improvements made. At the Sept-Iles reservation, the largest of all the Indian reservations in my constituency, there has been going on since last year a complete and total renovation of this reservation located within the very limits of this modern town which grew up and expanded through the mining developments that have occurred during the last ten years.
I also know that provision has been made to move the Schefferville Indian reservation for the greater good of this whole Indian community. However, there again, problems occur and this move will only take place when agreement is reached with the government of Quebec concerning lots, that is the land that is now owned by the crown.
There remain the Indian reservations on the lower north shore which are in a rather sorry state, not to say pitiful. These are the reservations of Mingan, Pointe-Parent and La Romaine and I hope the minister will duly note and that he will continue, as he has so well started, the improvement of the other reservations I mentioned a while ago.
I should also like to say a word about the improvements that were made to the Sept-Iles reservation, because, I said in 1956, while I was president of the chamber of commerce of that town, that the Indian reservation within the very city limits was in a deplorable condition, that there were a lot of slums and insanitary houses there and that such a

situation for Indians should not be tolerated any longer.
And I remember that at that time-I am still referring to 1956-we appealed to the minister. Indian affairs then came under the department of citizenship and immigration, which, if my memory serves me well, was then headed by the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill).
He came in person on the spot to assess the situation and he agreed that this situation was intolerable.
I am pleased to inform the house to-day that the minister realized that these improvements were a "must" and we are now satisfied with the results.
A little further up the north coast, as I mentioned earlier, there are several more Indian reserves in need of improvements. Some studies have been carried out in this area also, and I repeat once more I hope that the minister, who hears what I am saying, will take notice and will carry out the work to which he has given such a good start.
During the last year, Mr. Chairman, I received from various chiefs of Indian bands in my riding complaints concerning their responsibility.
They were complaining, and still are, that the government does not give them enough responsibility or freedom or, if you prefer, initiative. They are always told: The government will see to this or that, and Indian bands consider that they are thus deprived of their initiative.
Therefore, I think that as Indian bands are allowed to elect and appoint their chiefs-as is already done in a few reservations in my riding-who will be able to agree, understand and come to Ottawa-as has been done in the past-to exchange views with the departmental officials, it will then be possible to progressively delegate more responsibility and give more latitude to chiefs of Indian bands.
Mr. Chairman, there is another important matter which I would like to raise in this house today. Although it comes under provincial jurisdiction, on the one hand, it concerns also the federal government and more particularly the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
I received not very long ago a request from the employees of the federal government who work in the far north. They are posted on the shores of Ungava bay, Hudson strait and Hudson bay, all in the province of Quebec.
June 9, 1967

Following that request signed by several federal employees, here is what was published last May 18 in the Ottawa Citizen:
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)

It is entitled "2000 are deprived of franchise". I want to bring it to the attention of the minister because I think it is a big problem. The report from the Ottawa Citizen of May 18 reads as follows:
The Labrador boundary dispute between Quebec and Newfoundland has been depriving about 2,000 Quebeckers of a provincial franchise.
Involved are whites, Indians and Eskimos of voting age in most of the vast northern territory of new Quebec, formerly known as Ungava.
These people, except for residents of Schefferville and Fort Chimo, cannot vote in a provincial electoral riding.
They can vote federally in the riding of Saguenay but although they pay taxes to the province they are not yet represented in the Quebec legislature.
Several have complained to the tax appeal board of taxation without representation while the government works out a solution to a sensitive situation.
1927 DECISION
An official disclosed that if Quebec created a new riding in new Quebec without including Labrador the move would tend to undermine Quebec's claim on the disputed boundary.
Quebec does not accept as valid the British privy council decision of 1927, awarding Newfoundland the 110,000 square miles of Labrador wilderness.
Premier Daniel Johnson has established a four-man commission to examine the "territorial integrity" of Quebec, particularly the border with Newfoundland.
Chairman of the commission is Henri Dorion, a geographer from Laval University who argued in a 1963 book that the privy council decision is legally invalid.

Mr. Chairman, as I said earlier, I wanted to let the house know about that communication. I have here the federal employees' request which reads as follows:

As residents of the province of Quebec, we feel that we are the victims of an iniquitous situation and we would therefore like to enlist your assistance.
We are residents of a community in the far north of the province, and as such are levied all the provincial taxes such as income tax, sales tax, gasoline tax and so forth.
However, the government of Quebec has not seen fit to establish an electoral district in this area in order that we as bona fide residents of the province have the right to vote in provincial elections.
We have made previous attempts both personally and collectively to obtain satisfaction on this
Supply-Indian Affairs matter, with no results. In this connection we attach a copy of a letter dated April 24, 1967 which we wrote as a group to the Income Tax Appeal Board in Ottawa, copies of which were forwarded as noted thereon. We received a reply from this board dated May 2, 1967, which stated that the board had jurisdiction solely to hear appeals against income tax and estate tax, and that the matter raised in our letter was not within its jurisdiction.
The federal member for Saguenay, in whose federal riding we fall, contacted the Minister of National Revenue on the matter; we have received copies of the minister's reply to Mr. Blouin, wherein he stated that the matter was outside the jurisdiction of his department.
We have received nothing from either of the other recipients of copies of our letter of April 24.
As mentioned above, we have also been pursuing this question upon an individual basis, and we attach further a letter received by one of our group from the chief ruling officer of the provincial department of revenue dated May 16, 1967. As you will see from the third paragraph of this letter, the provincial department has ruled that the fact of residency is the deciding factor in taxation, not the right of representation. We feel that this is a point of doubtful moral legality, with its inference that we must pay all taxation without voice in the management of our affairs.
This letter goes on to state that "every resident of the province of Quebec is entitled to every benefit that the law may grant". In this community, we receive no provincial benefits whatsoever; all community services such as education, roads, power and medical treatment are provided by the federal government.
We must emphasize that we have no objection to the payment oi taxes per se. Indeed, we are merely using the fact of taxation as a vehicle for our protest. Our contention, which we must reiterate strongly, is that it is a situation of the utmost gravity in this day when a group of people can be denied the right to vote regarding the disposition of their affairs.
Quebec and Canada draw their heritage from two of the world's oldest democracies, England and France. England won the right of representation in 1215, and France in 1789. Surely, with this great heritage, we, residents of New Quebec in 1967, cannot accept this present situation without protest.
Here is the protest from the federal employees working in the far north. I had thought I would bring this matter up while we were studying the estimates of the department. Although, as I said before, this matter is under provincial jurisdiction, it is a big problem and I think something should be worked out in collaboration with the provincial government because there is absolutely no sense in the fact that in 1967 the people, even those working in the far north, should be deprived of the right to vote, which is so dear to every Canadian.

Mr. Chairman, I will limit my remarks in an effort to try to show some progress this afternoon. I merely want to refer to the use of the parks

June 9, 1967
Supply-Indian Affairs in the winter time. I am particularly interested in the Fundy national park in my constituency, but my thoughts might also be applied to the other maritime parks. I know that some work has been done in this field, but I feel that the department should conduct a full survey. I hate to advocate another investigation or survey for any department of the government, but I feel the time is approaching when we need a full investigation of the parks, particularly of the Fundy national park, in so far as any possible winter use is concerned.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
The park is a big thing for the area of New Brunswick in which Fundy is located. It is a tremendous hardship upon those who are dependent on the park to have a complete shutdown in September when the tourists leave. I know there are difficulties connected with winter operations. Someone asked "Do you have any visitors to Fundy national park in the wintertime?" The residents replied, "The only visitors we have are the moose that walk up and down the main street". It is that bad.
I know we investigated the possibility of opening a ski resort there a year or two ago, but it was found that would not be highly profitable. I suggest that the way people are moving around to different areas in the wintertime it might be possible to plan a skiing, curling and snowmobile resort. These things are very popular. I hope the minister will consider this appeal and have a through investigation made, during which the inhabitants will be consulted about the possibilities of the winter use of Fundy and other maritime parks.
My other thought concerns the new legislation. I believe the minister agrees with the thinking in New Brunswick in this regard. I have read one or two of his speeches and they seem to indicate quite progressive thinking. We have this park in New Brunswick which is, after all, the second smallest park. We need extra territory, and I suggest a coast line area so that we would have some beaches. This is one reason why the new legislation is necessary. I am not asking for a second national park in New Brunswick. There seem to be two points of view in the department in this regard. I hope that, in the light of the way the minister is thinking, Fundy national park will acquire additional areas along the coast line. This would give us an opportunity to have the Fundy vacation trail, and some beaches which we do not have now.

In closing, may I say I hope that, although I realize the minister has many other problems in his big department, he will not give the impression of not being as interested in the parks as he is in other branches of his department. I have been connected with this park in New Brunswick for 15 years. This is a sort of swan song because I am losing that area under redistribution. I was not around when the park was originally set up, so I cannot claim credit for that.
However, it has been a source of pride to visit the park each year and see the way it is progressing. During the time the Conservatives were in power they emphasized a scheme of winter works and park expansion. Some of this work has been continued but the impression is-I say this to the minister because I know he is a good politician and will want to correct it-that there has not been the same interest in the development of the park under the present administration. This may mean more money, and I suppose we will have to go along with that. The role of the park is changing. The length of stay for each visitor has gone down from 2.7 to 2.3 days recently. Quite a number of these commercial people have improved equipment, and I do not think we need to spend the money which we used to spend. I hope the minister will continue to foster interest in this family recreational park of Fundy.
I hope it will be possible for the parliamentary committee to visit the maritime parks now that they have that northern visit under their belts. I for one would welcome them to Fundy park in New Brunswick and would show them some of the delightful activities that can be undertaken there. For the information of members, a new branch of the liquor store has been opened in Alma, the heart of Fundy park, which indicates how progressive we are.

speechtext:
Having served as chairman of the committee on northern affairs and national resources, having had the privilege of leading 22 members of that committee on a two week visit to the north, from the eastern to the western Arctic, and having held hearings in western national parks, I feel I should say a few words of commendation to the minister for his very co-operative attitude. He has appeared before the committee at various times and given every bit of information asked of him, which was most useful to the committee. I should like also to express deep appreciation to the deputy minister and assistant deputy ministers for their assistance in
June 9, 1967

guiding the committee through their examination of the estimates, and for the arrangements made for our visits to the north and to the national parks.
I should like also to congratulate the minister upon his presentation of government policy in connection with national parks with which, notwithstanding some opposition to it, I heartily agree, and believe to be a policy which is acceptable to the overwhelming majority of Canadians. I heard the hon. member for Brandon-Souris make a very useful and classical presentation here this morning on this particular subject. We agree on many things, but there are one or two points concerning the leasehold proposition which may be debatable.
During our visits to the parks numerous presentations were received from many segments of our society regarding all aspects of park policy. Among all the submissions we received, there were several commending the government for its policy. I am not going to quote them all, but I am going to quote from the submission of the National and Provincial Parks Association of Canada. On page 8 of that submission, I find this:
As I realize your committee is concerned with the policy as it affects leases, I shall say a word about this.
We have studied both sides of this question to the best of our ability and have read statements by both Mr. Laing and the organized leaseholders.
It is most regrettable that the controversy over this issue has generated such extreme bitterness and ill will. In our view, this came about more because of a breakdown in communications than from any real objection to the government's policy per se.
Without going into the question of the legality of the government's proposals, there is no doubt in our minds that there is need for the crown to control leases more effectively than in the past in the interests of the Canadian people as a whole and taking into consideration the enormous and growing pressures on the use of parks. The idea that individuals should have the right to hold leases on cottages or summer homes in either national or provincial parks for their private use and enjoyment, no matter what the justification for it in the past, is an anachronism in this day and age. Doing away with such leases is a problem which some of the provinces have already faced up to. Ontario, for example, has for some time now been withdrawing leases as they fall due on cottages and commercial properties in Algonquin park. We support the government's policy to have eventually only those persons engaged in the
Supply-Indian Affairs administration of a park or the supply of necessary visitor services, and their dependants, as permanent park residents.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
We urge most strongly, however, that everything possible be done to avoid causing hardship to those affected by this new ruling. We are quite sure that the government intends to be fair, and will be fair in carrying out this policy. In view of the difficulties that have arisen with regard to leases, we believe that the government's proposal to set up a crown corporation to deal with this matter in future deserves consideration. Its terms of reference and the composition of its board of directors will need to be given most careful study, however, if the corporation is to function effectively and its influence kept within bounds. Great care will have to be taken if the corporation is established to see it is not able to wield power for which it does not have to account; nor must its powers enable it to influence policy in areas other than leasing. In other words, it must be an instrument for carrying out policy, not creating it.
A little bit of history may be appropriate at this point. When the first national park was established there was discussion in the House of Commons over proposed lease terms. Provision was made to grant leases for terms of 42 years with provision for repeated renewal-in other words, in perpetuity. Due, to a very great extent, to the very large capital expenditures by the federal government and to the enormous increase in park visitors, especially in recent years, the value of leasehold property has been greatly enhanced. As a result, sales of leasehold interests have often been made involving exorbitant profit to the leaseholder with no commensurate return to the landlord-the citizens of Canada. Today there are approximately 2,500 leases and licences of occupation in existence. Seventy per cent are old leases containing renewal clauses on expiration of each 42 years. Fourteen per cent are for 42 years, with provision for a single renewal for 21 years. The remaining 16 per cent have been issued since 1962 and are for 42 years or less without provision for renewal.
In all leases, the crown reserved certain rights, such as the prohibition of assignment without the written consent of the minister, and the right to review periodically the rent charged and to charge a rent equal to the annual value of the land.
The objectives of the national parks system are, first, to ensure the national park lands

June 9. 1967
Supply-Indian Affairs are passed on to future generations; second, to provide for the best use of the national parks consistent with their intended purpose; third, to serve the people in an effective and meaningful manner by helping them to understand and enjoy the parks; fourth, to encourage private enterprise to invest in and manage appropriate facilities for the visiting public inside and adjacent to parks, complementing governmental developments; and fifth, to expand the system adequately in every region of Canada.
I realize that among the many submissions we received from the residents of Banff and Jasper there may be some whose cases may deserve some special consideration. I am sure the minister is only too happy to take their cases into consideration.
Before I leave the question of national parks I would like to recommend to the minister that some serious consideration be given to the establishment of a national park in the lakehead region, where a beautiful chain of mountains, known as the great northwest, are situated almost at the gate of Fort William.
I have indicated to the minister the desire in this respect of the lakehead chamber of commerce, enthusiastically supported by the publisher of the Daily Times-Journal of Fort William, whose name is George Macgillivray, a member of the clan of Sir William Macgillivray, a governor of the Hudson Bay port in Fort William, after whom the city was named.
I am grateful to the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox for his kind remarks and for giving us a comprehensive and interesting report on the visit of the committee to the Canadian Arctic. His assessment of our visit demonstrated the co-operative and friendly spirit which animated every member of my committee.
Just a few words about the north, Mr. Chairman. During our visit to the north the committee held meetings at every point, from the east to the west, and the report which was presented to the house last September reveals some of the problems the remedying of which should present no difficulty to the government. One of these was the matter of radio and television, which the minister has indicated today will be taken care of gradually beginning with the T.V. station at Yellowknife.
One thing which was brought to the attention of the house by the hon. member for the Northwest Territories during the throne speech debate was the provision of water and

sewage services to the west end of the town of Inuvik, as the centre and east parts of the town are already serviced by utilidors.
There are many other questions that I could touch upon, but I see that there are other members anxious to speak on these estimates and I will therefore not prolong my remarks, except to say that the committee has served a useful purpose by visiting the far north and the western national parks, which now leaves the need for a visit to the eastern national parks which I hope the house will authorize to be made this fall.

the second reading of Bill No. C-9, to govern, license and regulate the operation of rainmaking equipment in Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the short title of this bill is a misnomer, because I am interested in legislation to deal with techniques which have recently been devised which affect the weather, and in that way constitute an interference with the weather enjoyed by individuals. It is
27053-88J
Licence for Rainmaking Equipment suggested that in these days the weather can be influenced by technology, which involves seeding clouds by the use of silver nitrate and iodine crystals, as well as other crystals which mix with the clouds, thus causing precipitation. The theory is that these crystals have an affinity for water, and if they are released into the air, under certain conditions with appropriate temperatures the molecules of water in clouds are drawn together with the molecules in the crystals; heavier water molecules are created and these, in turn, fall to the earth in the form of precipitation.
It is debatable whether one can make rain, though this subject has been discussed on the estimates of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I do not refer to the sort of rainmaking that the Indians engaged in with some success over the years. Hon. members may remember a court case on this continent that took place a few years ago, where the Indians were sued for large sums of money for causing a catastrophe by making rain. The Indians were hired to make rain; they were hired to make a reasonable amount of rain and the rain came, but it kept coming and coming. Eventually there was a flood and the Indians were sued because of the calamity that developed. Whether such a thing is possible I do not know, but I do know that it is possible, from scientific advances, to change atmospheric conditions so as to produce rain. Rain may be produced, provided other conditions are suitable.
Several departments of the provincial governments of Ontario and Quebec have been using rainmaking equipment to help to prevent forest fires. In Ontario, especially, a great deal of discussion has taken place in certain communities about the question of rainmaking. Several years ago the housewives of the Lake St. John area complained that, because of certain activity by the Department of Transport, they had not been able to dry their clothes for 60 days. In that period the sun never shone and it rained every day. The transport department at that time were conducting tests to determine the efficiency of rainmaking equipment in that area. The surprising thing is that when this activity stopped, after the housewives had complained, the weather cleared, the rain disappeared and fair weather followed immediately.
Hon. members may also remember what happened when the Ontario government used rainmaking equipment to solve some problems that farmers experienced. At that time there was a motion to adjourn the legislature
1376	COMMONS
Licence for Rainmaking Equipment under the special section which calls for the consideration of an immediate national problem. There was discussion about the drought which had been recurring over a period of years in the Renfrew area. The provincial government, to solve the difficulty, finally authorized $250,000 to be spent to hire a United States firm of rainmakers. It will be remembered, Mr. Speaker, that the firm brought its equipment to the Ottawa valley and-this may be taken as coming from Ripley's "Believe it or Not"-on that very day, when the matter was being discussed in the legislature, the rain began. The equipment was operating, though the company said that it had not influenced what happened on that day.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
The house may remember that the farmers were again in difficulty later on because the rain did not stop once it had started; they found themselves facing, not drought but an overabundance of moisture. Whether or not the rain making equipment in use today achieves the results which the farmers allege, I cannot claim to know with any certainty. In many of the areas where this equipment has been used the farmers claim there is a "yoyo" effect; the crystals are sent into the air by the use of a heat generator; they are carried by the clouds for a period before rain is produced, and then they fall back to the earth along with the rain. There are farmers who say that as soon as the sun comes out the crystals warm up, become lighter than air and rise into the clouds causing rain to fall again.
I know that in my own area where this equipment was used extensively some years back, no cloud passed over without some precipitation falling, even though in some cases it was very little. The department of lands and forests has been using these methods for some time, with limited success, as far as I know. The difficulty appears to be that after a cloud has been seeded the wind can change and the rain can fall where it is not needed.
This is what happened when the department seeded clouds for the purpose of dampening down forest fires. The prevailing wind changed and rain fell on agricultural land where it was not needed. This lack of assurance that rain will fall where it is intended to fall is another factor which affects the need to licence rain-making equipment. If this was a skilled science, as some of the companies operating this equipment would have us believe, it would be possible for a man to seed clouds in such a way that rain would fall on his neighbour's property. This is not possible. It

DEBATES	June 9, 1967
is all too likely to fall on his own property or on the wrong neighbour's property. This is not a field where provincial jursdiction is applicable. The winds know no boundaries and the results of this rain making are interprovincial in scope. For this reason I believe the federal government should assume responsibility for the control of the equipment used.
I am not proposing that rain making equipment should be prohibited. What I am proposing is that it should be licensed so that the government would have a measure of control over those who operate it and where it is used, in order to be in a position to judge whether rain falling in a given area had been brought about by those who were operating these machines and who might therefore be responsible for any damage caused to other parties.
In the example I gave, equipment was being operated in northern Ontario by the Ontario government's department of lands and forests. Damage was caused to agricultural communities which had no connection with that department at all. After it had been assessed the federal government had to make grants to assist farmers who had lost crops because of the continuing rain. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) was in the area at the time-an election was in progress-and he promised immediate relief to those concerned. Incidentally, this was not forthcoming. Indeed I wonder whether the federal government really had any responsibility; the fact that the provincial government took certain action is no reason for the federal government undertaking to pick up the tab.
The simple purpose of this bill is to licence, rainmaking equipment, thus allowing for records to be kept and the consequent assessment of any damage which might be claimed. Hon. members may say that this is not the responsibility of government. I would point out to them that in many parts of the country it is necessary to obtain a fire permit before burning any cover or brush during certain periods. A permit is required so that if a fire gets out of control the man responsible for it may be held liable for any damage caused.
There is not much difference between this and the circumstances I have been discussing. I believe everyone who has studied this subject agrees that it is possible to cause rain to fall in certain conditions. Provincial governments are certainly aware of the technical advances which have been made, otherwise they could not pay for rainmaking services

and equipment. Incidentally, when I talked to the minister of agriculture down in Ontario he told me they did not know what to do about the drought in the Renfrew area and had hired rainmaking equipment as a last resort. A year later he told me his department had still not been able to assess whether $250,000 of benefit had been received from that equipment or whether rain would have fallen anyway. But in order to satisfy the public and keep the farmers off their backs the department had undertaken this expense, with considerable success, it would appear; in fact it was greater than anticipated and, in the end, became a liability.
I know that some hon. members will take lightly this idea that rainmaking equipment should be licensed. Perhaps they have not looked into the technical aspects of this operation. If they do, they will probably be as interested as I am in some of the things which the professors and technicians have been accomplishing in this field. As I say, there is general agreement that in certain conditions rain can be induced to fall from clouds which otherwise would not have released rain in a given locality.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I think that most members, if they really think about the situation, will agree that the licensing and regulations which the government should establish around rainmaking equipment and which would be to the advantage of those operating the equipment and those who are paying for the use of the rainmaking equipment, would eliminate the valid objection by other people to the making of rain with this type of equipment. They will know that there is an avenue open to them to ascertain whether or not the equipment itself has been responsible for the creation of their damage and that there will be an opportunity for them to claim compensation for any damage caused to them as a result of the use of this equipment.
I do not expect that this bill will be passed today. We do not usually pass private members bills. I do suggest, however, that hon. members who are interested in agriculture, forestry and in fact in any control over our natural resources should be interested in the bill. I certainly would be pleased to support any government legislation which may flow from what I think is a new problem and one which will grow considerably with the technical advances that are being made in this particular field.
