Mr. Speaker, I am a little surprised that other members of the house are not in a rush to speak on this very interesting subject. I should like to say a few words in support of the bill which has been brought before us by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters). I was rather interested in the situation which developed in eastern Canada a while ago when the authorities of the province of Ontario undertook a program of seeking to induce rain by means of cloud seeding equipment. A few years ago similar events took place in the province of British Columbia, in the area of Canada which I represent in this house. At that time the then B.C. power commission and also the then Powell River company installed silver iodide generators for the purpose of inducing rainfall into the watershed areas which provide the source of supply for the dams for power purposes, in the case of the B.C. power commission, and for the supply of water for the production of pulp and paper in the case of the Powell River company.
So far as I know I was the first member ever to introduce this subject on the floor of the House of Commons. At least I had that impression from a discussion I had afterward with the then minister of justice, Hon. Stuart Garson. I may say, as a result of having raised this matter for the first time, among certain members of the house I was unofficially known by the nickname "Rainmaker". It was the then hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, Mr. Jack MacDougall, who tagged me with that label. He was rather fond of giving nicknames to members.
I should like to say that I raised the matter as a question which should receive consideration by the government because I expected, if this development continued, that the kind of problems which have been raised by the hon. member for Timiskaming in his speech, concerning the right of a certain individual or a corporation to take action which might affect the rights and well being of others, would arise.
I remember that I used the example of the farmer who had his hay out in the fields to dry when the B.C. power commission decided to precipitate rain in that particular area. In my view the potential infringement of the rights of the farmer was there. One question of course which immediately arises in a consideration of this kind, in a federal state such as ours, is as to where the jurisdiction lies. Is it a federal or a provincial matter? I argued
1378	COMMONS
Licence for Rainmaking Equipment then, and I argue still, that certainly the weatherman knows no provincial boundaries and that the conditions which create weather conditions, be they rain, sunshine, drought or flood, certainly are not confined within the boundaries of any individual province. It seems to me therefore that any legislation in this field probably lies within the jurisdiction of the federal authorities.
I think the proposal of my colleague that this regulation, through licence, should come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Transport, is an appropriate one, because as we all know the meteorological services which would provide the basic data on which to base any control or regulation come under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport. It is for that reason I believe this bill should receive serious consideration. I know there are questions which remain concerning the technical or technological efficacy of the various devices which have been used for cloud seeding, be they devices operated from the ground or devices used from airplanes in dispersing the silver iodide crystals which I understand are the generally used medium for helping the formation of the kind of water droplets which become heavy enough to be precipitated to the earth in the form of rain.
All too often it seems to me we have a tendency to lock the barn door after the horse has been stolen, as the old saying goes. In other words, in this chamber, we are not moved to the point of legislating until a situation involving serious damage or trouble has occurred. In view of the fact that we do know that there are established business concerns which are in the business of providing this service, and in view of the fact that we do know that provincial authorities and publicly owned corporations such as the B.C. power commission have taken this seriously enough to actually engage business firms to carry out this type of operation, it seems to me it would be quite appropriate that we should not be reluctant to agree to provide to a responsible jurisdiction control and licensing over such operations.
It is for these reasons that I thought I should like to say a few words in support of Bill No. C-9, which has been put before us by the hon. member for Timiskaming.

When we discuss a technical subject of this kind in the house during these last hours of the week, and if the subject is technical enough, some executive assistant is asked to go back and dig out the material that has been put together by experts of various departments in order to deal intelligently with the subject. In this way he can outline to hon. members what the government is doing and what the policy may be. In this particular case the government takes the subject quite seriously, and a considerable amount of work has taken place in the Department of Transport and in the meteorological branch in an attempt to follow the experiments of the emerging science of cloud seeding, and its importance in influencing rainfall. It is interesting to note that some of the material which has come into my hands as a result of drafting this effort this afternoon indicates the amount of material which is available to us on this subject.
I have a memo from which I should like to read a few sentences, because it helps to shed some light on the background of this subject. In part it states:
From 1959 to 1963 Inclusive, a precipitation physics project was carried on by the meteorological branch of the Department of Transport in the Rouyn-Noranda area of the province of Quebec.
That is an area in the neighbourhood of the riding of the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette). Members will recall that during
June 9, 1967

the last session of parliament this subject seemed to frighten the living daylights out of that gentleman from time to time, probably because he thought that the opposition was attempting to bring down thunderclouds on his head.
The memo then goes on to state that an aircraft was fitted out with instruments for taking physical measurements of precipitation mechanisms, and at the same time to conduct an investigation to evaluate the effect of cloud seeding. The memo states:
Two areas in Quebec, along the border of Ontario in the vicinity of Rouyn-Noranda, were chosen for these cloud seeding experiments. The areas were approximately 35 miles square and 35 miles apart., . On suitable occasions, clouds already producing rain upwind of one of the test areas were seeded with silver iodide. The clouds upwind from the other area were not seeded, so that a comparison could be made of the rain that fell in the seeded area and that which fell in the unseeded control area.
From 1959 to 1963, 54 cloud and rain situations were seeded with silver iodide. Seeding was carried on for a total of 173 hours and 19 minutes. Forty five of these cases were found suitable for analysis, and the rainfall from these situations was compared statistically.
The memo then goes on to say:
However, it appears that the chances of making large changes in rainfall by this method are very slight. As expressed by the statisticians, the probability of an increase or decrease in rainfall greater than 22 per cent was found to be less than 1 in 20.
There appears to be something less than a good chance of making rain, not even great enough to frighten the nervous member for Villeneuve. The memo then continues:
Because of the large natural variability of rainfall it was found to be impossible to be more precise about the effects of seeding. These results are similar to those found in most other carefully controlled tests of cloud seeding such as have been carried out in Australia and the United States.
That was not an isolated expression of an attempt to gain knowledge by the Canadian meteorological department on this subject. There is a considerable amount of information on the subject contained in government pamphlets, samples of which I have. The first was dated December 1, 1965, under the title "Cloud seeding to influence rainfall-it's importance and present status" written by C. L. Crozier and J. D. Holland. It is interesting to note in this particular pamphlet that experiments have been going on all around the world regarding this very interesting subject. Field experiments have taken place in Argentina and statistical evaluations have been made there.

Since 1947 Australia has been undertaking fundamental studies of physical processes occurring in clouds. In France about ten French organizations are working on various facets of artificial weather modification, closely related with basic cloud physics studies. Israel has conducted field experiments and laboratory studies on artificial cloud modification for many years. After a number of years of experiments, Italy has now begun a program which is attempting to solve, on a practical basis, the problem of control and evaluation of the results of seeding cumuliform clouds. Two groups in Japan with weather modification interests have experimented with ground based and balloon borne silver iodide generation, and experiments are being carried out in Mexico as well as in the U.S.S.R. and in communist China. There is also a considerable amount of experimentation taking place in the United States. From all this one can see that there is interest throughout the world in this subject.
In view of this great interest throughout the world perhaps the time has come, as the hon. member suggested today in introducing his bill, to think in terms of what may be needed should rainmaking become a science through which it is possible to precipitate moisture in sizable quantities under control. If this could be done all sorts of problems might be created in relation to when, to what extent, and through which company, corporations or municipalities, rain should be created.
This bill is perhaps timely because we should give some thought to this subject and keep in touch with the experiments that are being made in this field. Perhaps it would be a good idea to have the subject matter of this bill referred to the transport committee. That committee would then have the opportunity of calling upon government experts and outside witnesses in order to gain some comprehension of what is involved.

There is another aspect of making the earth fertile that will undoubtedly come to us more quickly than rainmaking. I think that making the land fertile will come in the movement of rivers and with irrigation projects generated therefrom. I believe this is a field we should be studying concurrently with such matters as rainmaking, because it is becoming more and more important to learn how to govern the water and moisture available to us in a world increasing in population and aridity.
One of the things you notice when flying westward over old Toronto is the way in which the forest has been denuded. The land now appears quite arid. This is especially so in midsummer. I am sure that in our fathers' and grandfathers' time this condition did not exist. There was then much swampland, much forestland, and the temperature and humidity were different because of the tree coverage and the retention of moisture therefrom. As we fly over and look down at the great lakes we see around the rim of the lakes the receding shoreline and the evidence of widening beaches. We then realize that the water tables of the continent are sinking as a result of decreasing forest cover, swampland and the moist areas which the forests retain. I think this should be an important part of our studies in learning to husband the resources of water on this continent.
We in the west are very concerned about these matters because we have the privilege of living in an area of a great amount of water and see to the south, in the arid desert land of the United States, people who would like to move this water into their areas in order to water the deserts and make them green. When one considers the Middle East problem which faces this house today I think you will find that a great deal of the problem arises from their difficulties with regard to water and moisture, the subject we are talking about today. We find that the nations experimenting with rainmaking, all forms of irrigation and methods of producing moisture for their lands-this is the case in the Middle East-are very much worried about how they will cultivate the soil for their increasing populations.
This is a very all-embracing and important subject. It is one to which we in the House of Commons should address ourselves in several ways. Even as a pinch-hitter this afternoon, with no expertise on the subject, I realize, as I think all hon. members do, that this question is vitally important to us and deserves serious consideration.

Scientific research has progressed to the point where, today, rainmaking machines may turn out to be the answer to the disasters caused by hurricanes.
